是 (shì) is the affirmative verb meaning 'to be' or 'yes', used to confirm a statement or identity.
对 (duì) means 'correct' or 'right', used to affirm that something is true or accurate.
不对 (bú duì) means 'not correct' or 'wrong', formed by placing 不 (bù) before 对 (duì) to negate it.
好的 (hǎo de) is a casual way to say 'okay' or 'alright', expressing agreement or acknowledgment.
好的 (hǎo de) is used to express agreement or to say 'okay', with 的 (de) softening the tone and making it more casual.
什么 (shénme) is the question word for 'what', used to ask about objects, things, or information.
谁 (shéi) is the question word for 'who', used to ask about a person or identity.
什么 (shénme) asks about things or information.
哪里 (nǎlǐ) asks about a location or place.
为什么 (wèishénme) literally means 'for what' and is used to ask 'why', combining 为 (for/because) and 什么 (what).
怎么 (zěnme) asks about the manner or method of something, meaning 'how'.
为什么 (wèishénme) asks for a reason or cause, meaning 'why'.
多少 (duōshao) asks about quantity or amount, meaning 'how many' or 'how much'.
我是学生 (wǒ shì xuésheng) is a basic identity sentence: 我 (I) + 是 (am) + 学生 (student), following the Subject-Verb-Object structure.
请坐 (qǐng zuò) is a polite invitation to sit down, with 请 (please) making the command courteous.
请站起来 (qǐng zhàn qǐlái) politely asks someone to stand up.
你是老师吗 (nǐ shì lǎoshī ma) turns a statement into a yes/no question by adding 吗 (ma) at the end.
早上好 (zǎoshang hǎo) is the standard morning greeting.

晚安 (wǎn ān) is used to say good night.
对不起 (duìbuqǐ) literally means 'cannot face you', used to apologize.
不客气 (bú kèqi) means 'don't be polite', the standard response to 谢谢 (thank you).
谢谢 (xièxie) is the common way to say thank you.
你好吗 (nǐ hǎo ma) turns the greeting 你好 into a question by adding 吗 (ma).
你叫什么名字 (nǐ jiào shénme míngzi) asks for someone's name.
再见 (zàijiàn) means 'see you again', the standard farewell expression.
谁 (shéi) is used to ask about a person's identity.
什么 (shénme) is the interrogative word for asking about things or information.
哪里 (nǎlǐ) asks about a location or place.
不是 (bú shì) is the negation of 是, used to say 'no' or 'it is not'.
好的 (hǎo de) expresses agreement or acknowledgment, meaning 'okay' or 'alright'.
对 (duì) affirms that something is correct or right.
一 (yī) is the number one, the simplest character in Chinese, represented by a single horizontal stroke.
二 (èr) means two, written with two horizontal strokes.
三 (sān) means three, written with three horizontal strokes.
四 (sì) means four.
四 (sì) means four; its tone is fourth (falling), so pronounce it with a sharp downward pitch.
五 (wǔ) means five, pronounced with a third (dipping) tone.
六 (liù) means six and uses a fourth (falling) tone.
七 (qī) means seven and is pronounced with a first (flat high) tone.
七 (qī) means seven; it has a first tone, so keep your pitch high and level when saying it.
八 (bā) means eight; it is considered a lucky number in Chinese culture.
九 (jiǔ) means nine and is pronounced with a third (dipping) tone.
十 (shí) means ten and looks like a plus sign.
十 (shí) means ten; shaped like a cross, it combines a vertical and horizontal stroke to represent a complete set of ten.
十一 (shí yī) is formed by combining 十 (ten) and 一 (one), literally meaning ten-one, which equals eleven.
十七 (shíqī) means seventeen.
十八 (shíbā) means eighteen.
十九 (shíjiǔ) means nineteen, formed by ten (十) plus nine (九).
二十 (èrshí) means twenty, literally two-tens.
四十四 (sìshísì) means forty-four.
四十五 (sìshíwǔ) means forty-five.
四十六 (sìshíliù) means forty-six.
五十 (wǔshí) means fifty, literally five-tens.
八十七 (bāshíqī) means eighty-seven.
八十八 (bāshíbā) means eighty-eight; doubly lucky in Chinese culture.
八十九 (bāshíjiǔ) means eighty-nine.
九十九 (jiǔshíjiǔ) means ninety-nine; symbolically associated with longevity in Chinese culture.
星期一 (xīngqī yī) means Monday; 星期 means week or weekday, and 一 (one) indicates it is the first day of the week.
星期二 (xīngqī èr) means Tuesday.
星期三 (xīngqī sān) means Wednesday.
星期四 (xīngqī sì) means Thursday.
星期四 (xīngqī sì) means Thursday.
星期五 (xīngqī wǔ) means Friday.
星期六 (xīngqī liù) means Saturday.
星期六 (xīngqī liù) means Saturday; 六 (six) is used because Saturday is the sixth day in the Chinese weekly count starting from Monday.
现在几点 (xiànzài jǐ diǎn) means 'what time is it now?'; 现在 means now, 几 asks how many, and 点 means o'clock.
一点 (yī diǎn) means one o'clock; 点 is used after the hour number to express a specific hour.
两点 (liǎng diǎn) means two o'clock; note that 两 (liǎng) is used instead of 二 (èr) when telling time.
三点 (sān diǎn) means three o'clock.
上午 (shàngwǔ) means morning or AM, literally 'above noon', while 下午 (xiàwǔ) means afternoon or PM, literally 'below noon'.
分 (fēn) means minute when telling time.
小时 (xiǎoshí) means hour as a duration.
秒 (miǎo) means second as a unit of time.
一月 (yī yuè) means January; Chinese months are named by number followed by 月 (month), making them easy to remember.
五月 (wǔ yuè) means May, the fifth month.
六月 (liù yuè) means June, the sixth month.
七月 (qī yuè) means July, the seventh month.
这个月 (zhège yuè) means this month; 这个 is the demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this', and 月 means month.
这个月 (zhège yuè) means this month.
上个月 (shàng gè yuè) means last month.
下个月 (xià gè yuè) means next month.
爸爸 (bàba) is the informal, everyday word for 'dad' or 'father' in Mandarin, commonly used in casual family settings rather than the more formal 父亲 (fùqīn).
哥哥 (gēge) means 'older brother' and is used to address or refer to an elder male sibling; Mandarin distinguishes elder and younger siblings with different words.
姐姐 (jiějie) means 'older sister' and is the counterpart to 哥哥; it specifically refers to a female sibling who is older than the speaker.
孩子 (háizi) is a general term for 'child' or 'children' and can refer to offspring of any age when used by parents in conversation.
姐姐 (jiějie) refers specifically to an elder sister; Mandarin uses separate vocabulary for older versus younger siblings, reflecting the cultural emphasis on birth order.
朋友 (péngyou) is the standard Mandarin word for 'friend'; it can refer to any close companion and is widely used in both formal and informal contexts.
男朋友 (nán péngyou) literally means 'male friend' but is used to mean 'boyfriend'; 男 (nán) adds the male gender to 朋友 (péngyou).
女朋友 (nǚ péngyou) literally means 'female friend' and is used to say 'girlfriend'; 女 (nǚ) specifies the female gender in this compound.
朋友 (péngyou) on its own simply means 'friend' without any gender specification, contrasting with 男朋友 and 女朋友 which imply a romantic relationship.
同事 (tóngshì) combines 同 (tóng, 'same/together') and 事 (shì, 'work/matter') to mean someone who works alongside you — a colleague or coworker.
同事 (tóngshì) means 'colleague', formed from 同 (same/together) and 事 (work), referring to someone you share a workplace with.
朋友 (péngyou) means 'friend' and is a general term for a companion, distinct from a neighbor or coworker.
邻居 (línjū) means 'neighbor', combining 邻 (lín, 'adjacent/nearby') and 居 (jū, 'to reside'), describing someone who lives close to you.
高 (gāo) is a versatile adjective meaning 'tall' when describing people and 'high' when describing objects or levels; it is also commonly used in compound words like 高兴 (gāoxìng, happy).
瘦 (shòu) describes someone as 'thin' or 'slim'; it is the direct opposite of 胖 (pàng) and can sometimes carry a neutral or even positive connotation depending on context.
高 (gāo) means 'tall' when used to describe a person's height, contrasting with 矮 (ǎi, short) in the physical description vocabulary.
胖 (pàng) means 'fat' or 'chubby' and is the opposite of 瘦 (shòu, thin); in Chinese culture it can sometimes be used affectionately, though context matters greatly.
瘦 (shòu) is the adjective for 'thin' or 'slim' used to describe body type; it directly contrasts with 胖 (pàng, fat) and is a key descriptor in physical appearance vocabulary.
漂亮 (piàoliang) means 'beautiful' or 'pretty' and is one of the most common compliments in Mandarin; it can describe people, objects, or even actions done skillfully.
矮 (ǎi) describes short stature and is the opposite of 高 (gāo, tall); it is used specifically for height, not for other kinds of shortness.
瘦 (shòu) refers to a slim or thin physique and is the antonym of 胖 (pàng); it is commonly used when describing someone's body shape.
医生 (yīshēng) means 'doctor', combining 医 (yī, medicine) and 生 (shēng, person); it is used for physicians in general and is a respectful, common term in everyday speech.

商人 (shāngrén) combines 商 (shāng, business/trade) and 人 (rén, person) to mean 'businessman' or 'merchant'; the suffix 人 is commonly used in Mandarin to denote a person engaged in a particular profession or from a certain place.
学生 (xuésheng) means 'student', formed from 学 (xué, to study) and 生 (sheng, person); it is used for students at any educational level from primary school to university.
工程师 (gōngchéngshī) means 'engineer', combining 工程 (gōngchéng, engineering/project) and 师 (shī, skilled master); 师 is a respectful suffix used for experts like teachers (老师) and engineers.
商人 (shāngrén) is composed of 商 (shāng, commerce/trade) and 人 (rén, person), literally 'a person of commerce', and refers to a businessman or merchant engaged in trade.
米饭 (mǐfàn) combines 米 (mǐ, rice grain) and 饭 (fàn, cooked food) to specifically mean cooked white rice; 饭 alone can also mean 'meal' broadly, making 米饭 more precise when referring to steamed rice.

饺子 (jiǎozi) are the classic Chinese dumplings with a thin dough wrapper and savory filling; 子 (zi) is a common noun suffix in Mandarin, and 饺子 are especially popular during Chinese New Year celebrations.
包子 (bāozi) are fluffy steamed buns filled with meat or vegetables; 包 (bāo) means 'to wrap', reflecting the way the dough wraps around the filling.

汤 (tāng) means 'soup' or 'broth' and is a staple of Chinese cuisine; it appears in many dish names and is an essential part of Chinese meals, often served at the end of a meal in traditional settings.
包子 (bāozi) are soft steamed buns filled with pork, vegetables, or sweet fillings; 包 (bāo) reflects the wrapping action used to make them, and they are a beloved street food across China.
水 (shuǐ) is one of the most fundamental characters in Mandarin, meaning 'water'; it also serves as a radical in many water-related characters and is essential vocabulary for everyday life.
水 (shuǐ) means 'water' and is a single-character word; it is the base for many drink names in Chinese and one of the first characters learners should recognize.
茶 (chá) means 'tea' and is deeply embedded in Chinese culture; China is the birthplace of tea, and the word 茶 has spread to many world languages through trade routes like the Silk Road.
咖啡 (kāfēi) is a phonetic transliteration of 'coffee'; both characters were chosen for their sounds rather than meanings, a common method in Mandarin for borrowing foreign words.

果汁 (guǒzhī) literally means 'fruit liquid', combining 果 (guǒ, fruit) and 汁 (zhī, juice/liquid); it is the standard term for fruit juice and can be preceded by the fruit name, e.g. 橙汁 (chéngzhī, orange juice).
咖啡 (kāfēi) is a loanword transliterated from English 'coffee'; the characters were selected purely for phonetic similarity and carry no independent meaning related to the beverage.
果汁 (guǒzhī) means 'fruit juice', made up of 果 (guǒ, fruit) and 汁 (zhī, liquid/juice); it is a transparent compound whose meaning is evident from its individual characters.

啤酒 (píjiǔ) means 'beer', combining the phonetic borrowing 啤 (pí, from 'beer') with the native word 酒 (jiǔ, alcoholic beverage); 酒 alone refers to any alcoholic drink and appears in many beverage names.
我要 (wǒ yào) means 'I want' and is a fundamental phrase for ordering food or requesting items; 要 (yào) can mean 'want', 'need', or 'will', making it one of the most versatile verbs for beginners.
好吃 (hǎochī) literally means 'good to eat' and is the standard expression for 'delicious'; this pattern of 好 + verb is productive in Mandarin, e.g. 好喝 (hǎohē, delicious to drink).
不辣 (bú là) means 'not spicy', where 不 (bù) is the standard negation word and 辣 (là) means 'spicy'; the tone of 不 changes to bú before a 4th-tone syllable, which is why it is pronounced bú là.
买单 (mǎidān) literally means 'buy the bill' and is used to ask for the check at a restaurant; it is a common Cantonese-influenced expression widely used across Mandarin-speaking regions.
好吃 (hǎochī) means 'delicious' and is formed by combining 好 (hǎo, good) with 吃 (chī, eat); it is the go-to compliment for food in Mandarin and is understood throughout all Chinese-speaking regions.

这个多少钱 (zhège duōshao qián) is the essential shopping phrase meaning 'How much is this?'; it combines 这个 (zhège, this), 多少 (duōshao, how much/many), and 钱 (qián, money) — a must-know sentence for any market visit.
贵 (guì) means 'expensive' and also carries the meaning of 'precious' or 'honorable'; when shopping, it is commonly used in phrases like 太贵了 (tài guì le, too expensive) during bargaining.

便宜 (piányì) means 'cheap' or 'inexpensive'; interestingly, 便 (pián) in this compound has a different pronunciation and meaning than its standalone reading, showing how Mandarin characters can shift in tone and meaning in compounds.
打折 (dǎzhé) means 'discount', literally 'to fold the price'; in Chinese pricing, discounts are expressed as fractions of 10, so 打八折 (dǎ bā zhé) means an 80% price, i.e. a 20% discount.
打折 (dǎzhé) means 'to give a discount' or 'on sale'; 打 (dǎ) is a versatile verb meaning 'to do/hit' and 折 (zhé) means 'fold', together creating the concept of 'folding down' the price.
